rationale: The December 2022 review included 18 articles covering 291 Parkinson psychosis participants and 433 comparison participants. Psychosis includes hallucinations or delusions and the reported outcomes concern imaging. The 2024 Brain Communications paper is an expanded version of the same registered review, CRD42020221904. Neither version records oral dried figs or food-timed visual episode counts.

Abstract 4 follows 26 pimavanserin recipients, including 21 with Parkinson disease, using neuropsychiatric and quality-of-life measures. Abstract 36 compares 3-day dietary records among 24 Parkinson outpatients grouped by sarcopenia. These are separate studies. The diet study analyzes overall protein intake without a named dried fig exposure or a visual hallucination outcome.

EPR-016 assesses liquid meal and octreotide blood pressure responses in autonomic failure, including eight Parkinson patients within a sample of 67. EPR-203 compares FDG PET and questionnaire or task measures in 11 Parkinson patients with visual symptoms and nine without. Neither member assigns dried figs, and the two outcome sets come from separate patients.

EPO-049 compares resting EEG microstates in 19 Parkinson patients with hallucinations and 20 matched patients. EPO-553 compares task-evoked EEG in 23 Parkinson patients with minor hallucinations and 23 without. Resting microstate transitions and evoked processing are different measures. The posters contain no assigned or measured dried fig intake.

OP-592 uses cardiac MIBG imaging in 95 people with mild cognitive impairment. Abnormal scans occur in 22 of 37 probable Lewy body cases and normal scans in 38 of 43 Alzheimer-type cases, matching the later main cohort paper. Visual hallucinations contribute to the clinical classification. Cardiac tracer findings neither record dried fig exposure nor count recurrent visual episodes after eating.

The study compares cerebral hypo- and hypermetabolic patterns and their relationships to baseline cognitive performance in 55 participants with dementia with Lewy bodies. The underlying scans and cognitive scores do not give a dried fig comparison or clinical visual episode incidence.

The original compares genome-wide DNA methylation in cerebellar tissue from pathologically confirmed dementia with Lewy bodies and control donors. Its tissue and pathway analyses do not describe a dietary intervention or follow visual hallucinations after eating.

The original relates serum neurofilament to disability milestones, clinical deterioration and mortality in Parkinson disease. A milestone or reported symptom status marks progression. The design does not compare dried fig intake or record visual episodes relative to meals.

The paper discusses how to apply invasive-treatment recommendations to differing Parkinson phenotypes. Clinical selection and complications, including concerns in patients with psychosis, address device or drug management. There is no original culinary comparison.

The 37-week open-label trial compares istradefylline with a strategy without istradefylline and measures progression in levodopa requirements. Motor and nonmotor scores and adverse-event observations belong to those medication strategies. The trial neither assigns figs nor estimates food-timed visual episode frequency.

The clinicopathological study examines tau epitopes representing different stages of tangle maturation in brains grouped by Lewy body and Alzheimer pathology. The tissue contrasts and corresponding clinical classification provide no dried fig exposure or frequency after ingestion.

The review synthesizes screening and management approaches, including care for cognitive and psychiatric symptoms in Lewy body dementia. Its treatment discussion and symptom overview do not provide an original dried fig or visual episode-frequency comparison.

The clinical report and literature review consider X-linked PGK1-associated parkinsonism and epilepsy and a levodopa response. The genetic syndrome, reported medication experience and symptom history provide no dried fig exposure measure.

The review includes 55 reports and assesses relationships between psychiatric comorbidity and later Parkinson outcomes. Psychosis definitions and prognostic outcomes are broader than recurrent visual hallucinations. None of its pooled comparisons tests eating dried figs.

The researchers integrate protein-interaction and transcriptomic data to identify gene clusters shared or distinguished across Parkinson disease and schizophrenia. A comorbidity mechanism inferred from networks does not supply a measured food exposure or clinical episode count.

This clinical guidance describes continuous subcutaneous foslevodopa and foscarbidopa for motor fluctuations and draws on the existing trial reports. Hallucination discussion concerns dopaminergic treatment and adverse-event management. It does not report an independent food-exposure cohort.

The review discusses registered and observational evidence on proton pump inhibitor exposure and dementia or cognitive outcomes. The exposures are medications or clinical comorbidities. There is no dried fig intervention or longitudinal visual hallucination count.

The original combines alpha-synuclein seed amplification and other CSF biomarkers to distinguish pathological processes along the Lewy body and Alzheimer spectra. Disease classification and assay discrimination do not measure oral dried fig or repeated visual symptoms.

The meta-analysis uses data from three double-blind randomized donepezil comparisons in dementia with Lewy bodies. The NPI-2 combines hallucinations and cognitive fluctuations. This drug outcome is broader than visual episode frequency and contains no dried fig comparison.

The study elicits recognizable forms in ambiguous stimuli from stroke patients and controls. Counts in a stimulus task measure perceptual interpretation, with lesion hemisphere as a grouping variable. The counts do not represent spontaneous Parkinson visual hallucinations after dried figs.

The full analysis examines 263 dementia with Lewy bodies patient–caregiver pairs, clinical department, and physicians' awareness of treatment needs. It characterizes symptom and care priorities. The later quality-of-life analysis reuses the survey, without food intake or food-timed hallucination recording.

The HoRC-MSA series applies diagnostic criteria for multiple system atrophy and examines how clinical characteristics affect classification. Hallucinations are relevant to differential diagnosis. There is no measured dried fig exposure or Parkinson visual episode comparison.

The original review compares patterns and overlaps in tau and alpha-synuclein disorders. Pathological classification of diseases provides no dried fig versus comparator intervention or follow-up of visual hallucinations timed to intake.

This archived review discusses GABA-related motor and nonmotor mechanisms across Parkinson disease. Neurochemical pathway and treatment context supply no ordinary dried fig ingestion or a resulting visual hallucination series.

The authors discuss recognizing illusions, hallucinations and delusions and summarize use of pimavanserin and other treatment strategies. These are psychiatric symptom and drug-management data. The article does not compare dried fig consumption or measure visual frequency as a food response.

The review examines the roles of inflammatory mediators, peripheral immune processes and glia in neurodegenerative disorders. Its cellular and pathological framing provides no fig-specific oral exposure or observed visual events.

The cross-sectional multicenter analysis uses structural imaging to compare grey matter networks in women and men with dementia with Lewy bodies. Image-derived network patterns are the comparison. Participants' dried fig intake is not an exposure in the analysis.

This review examines treatment research for inherited glucocerebrosidase deficiency and its relevance to Gaucher disease. The disease and candidate therapy discussion is separate from an oral culinary exposure or a visual hallucination outcome in Parkinson disease.

The investigators survey German geriatric departments about which standardized instruments they use. The unit of observation is the department's assessment practice. No participants are compared on dried fig intake or Parkinson visual hallucinations.

The article discusses management and existing evidence for heterogeneous behavioral and psychiatric symptoms in dementia. Its recommendations and trial examples provide psychosis context without an original dried fig exposure or separately measured Parkinson visual episodes.

The systematic review summarizes dopamine transporter imaging in atypical and less common movement disorders, including disorders outside idiopathic Parkinson disease. It evaluates clinical utility of imaging rather than food-linked symptom frequency.

The study examines brain tissue markers of microglial and astrocytic activity across dementia with Lewy bodies and Alzheimer co-pathology. It relates microglial reactivity to amyloid and phosphorylated tau without measuring oral dried fig intake or visual event frequency.

This clinical series describes cognitive and motor manifestations in genetically characterized Huntington disease-like 2, including atypical presentations of bradykinesia or rigidity. These are a separate disorder and genotype; there is no dried fig or Parkinson visual hallucination comparison.

The review considers whether subjective experiences during classic psychedelic use explain subsequent changes in psychiatric outcomes. The exposures and acute perceptual changes pertain to pharmacologic agents; the review contains no dried fig challenge in Parkinson disease.

This clinical comparison measures peripheral inflammatory biomarkers in neurodegenerative groups and controls. Diagnostic cytokine patterns supply a biomarker contrast without a dried fig exposure or an episode count.

The review describes clinical variants, neuropathology and treatment of progressive supranuclear palsy. Differential-diagnosis signs and proposed mechanisms do not comprise a dried fig or a recurring Parkinson visual symptom measurement.

The original measures pantothenic acid in 20 dementia with Lewy bodies and 19 control donors, with lower concentrations in six of ten regions, including primary visual cortex. It mentions visual hallucinations as a possible interpretation of the anatomy. Food composition separately confirms that dried figs contain this nutrient. The tissue comparison has no individual food intake, supplementation, or clinical episode counts.

The authors use the previously reported multicenter patient and caregiver survey to investigate factors associated with quality of life in probable dementia with Lewy bodies. The treatment-needs paper is part of the same source family. The derived questionnaire analysis does not record a dried fig exposure or isolate recurrent food-timed visual events.

The review synthesizes radionuclide imaging findings relevant to cognition and dementia in Parkinson disease. It discusses regional metabolism and transmitter systems and variability among studies. No included exposure contrast bears on ordinary dried figs and visual hallucination frequency.

The review attributes forms of parkinsonism to mitochondrial maintenance and dynamics defects and discusses associated diagnostic features. Genetic and phenotype comparisons do not assess the claimed culinary exposure or visual episode response.

The model paper links the Gba1 E326K variant to enzyme activity, substrate accumulation, behavior and tissue pathology. Nonmotor test outcomes in the experimental model do not record human visual hallucinations or dried fig intake.

The original assesses pathological alpha-synuclein signals as a prodromal synucleinopathy marker. Clinical classifications and biofluid assay results supply the comparison and do not measure dried fig consumption or visual symptom response.

The investigators compare HEp-2 autoantibody patterns in samples from Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy and dementia with Lewy bodies. The serum or plasma immunofluorescence patterns do not measure oral fig exposure or count hallucinations after food.

The review considers defects in secretory and trafficking pathways in Parkinson disease, including genetic and cellular evidence. It contains no actual study of dried fig intake or clinical visual hallucination episode counts.

The analysis covers 624 participants with dementia and distinguishes reported visual impairment from measured near acuity. Neuropsychiatric outcomes are questionnaire measures and not meal-linked observations. There is no dried fig exposure or Parkinson-specific treatment effect in this analysis.

The review compares structural, functional and molecular imaging features used to distinguish Parkinson disease from atypical syndromes. Visual image features and diagnostic criteria do not form a visual hallucination outcome following dried figs.

The narrative review concerns music interventions, affect, cognition and neurological rehabilitation. It summarizes music rather than a dietary treatment, with no dried fig exposure or repeated visual hallucination count tied to diet.

The paper trains and interprets machine-learning models for early Parkinson detection using Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative data. Classification performance and input importance do not assess a food-related symptom response.

The clinical report evaluates Bálint syndrome and whether this visuospatial phenotype relates to disease progression in dementia with Lewy bodies. Recurrent visual hallucinations are part of the clinical context. Visuospatial test failures do not count food-timed visual events.

The authors discuss computational models that integrate heterogeneous disease mechanisms and data. The modeled pathways do not provide an original measured oral dried fig comparison or clinical hallucination follow-up.

TMS-evoked potentials compare cortical responses after stimulating motor, prefrontal and visual regions in Parkinson disease and comparison participants. Occipital network responses are evoked physiology. The study does not measure meal-associated visual hallucinations or record dried fig exposure.

The reappraisal compares MRI-derived cholinergic basal forebrain measures with cognition in Parkinson disease. Regional measurements and cognitive outcomes do not test eating dried figs or repeated visual hallucinations.

The online study groups respondents by reported hallucination content across senses and derives four clusters. Its survey outcome is a profile of content and experiences. It supplies no Parkinson-specific dried fig exposure or food-timed event count.

The review discusses autonomic, motor and cerebellar features and diagnostic workup for multiple system atrophy. Symptoms guide differentiation from other syndromes. There is no recorded dried fig intake or comparison of recurrent visual episodes after food.

The study compares Parkinson dementia patient and caregiver ratings in 21 dyads. Agreement for the SAPS-PD summary score is ICC 0.464, with poor agreement on six of nine items. The source is directly relevant to whose report a symptom scale captures, but neither reporter supplies a food-timed dried fig comparison.

The systematic review compares sexes across Parkinson disease, Parkinson dementia and dementia with Lewy bodies. The analysis groups neuropsychiatric measures, including psychosis-related outcomes. Sex is a comparison variable and dried fig intake is unmeasured.

This original compares psychopathology dimensions with neurobiological responses during viewing of affective stimuli. Late positive potential reflects emotional reactivity in a task; it does not count spontaneous visual hallucinations in Parkinson disease after food.

The study evaluates substantia nigra echogenicity and ventricular size as possible early dementia with Lewy bodies markers. Sonographic markers and clinical diagnosis are the comparison. No dried fig ingestion or food-timed clinical symptom effect is measured.

This overview combines findings of systematic reviews and meta-analyses of biomarkers associated with cognitive impairment. Its Parkinson, Lewy body dementia and multiple system atrophy groups support diagnostic or prognostic context without exposure-specific visual episode data.

The published review reports 29 articles and 1,367 participants, of whom 514 had psychosis and 853 did not. It shares PROSPERO CRD42020221904 with the 2022 preprint. Imaging comparisons include heterogeneous hallucination and delusion definitions and no dried fig ingestion outcome.

The researchers measure locus coeruleus MRI differences between mild cognitive impairment with Lewy bodies and healthy controls. These measures evaluate neurodegeneration and diagnosis; the study does not track visual episodes after eating dried figs.

The original compares rare whole-genome sequence variants in dementia with Lewy bodies. Diagnostic features help define cases; sequencing does not quantify clinical visual symptoms after dried fig intake.

Twelve dementia with Lewy bodies participants enter a single sequence of four placebo weeks, eight active ultrasound weeks and four follow-up weeks. The study evaluates a device and clinical tolerability. It includes no oral dried fig comparison and cannot estimate a culinary effect.

The study uses standing balance features among 210 enrolled participants to identify Parkinson disease or separate clinical stages. Postural measures and diagnostic model performance do not represent visual hallucination episodes after eating.

The authors compare white matter hyperintensity burden and basal forebrain cholinergic degeneration in Alzheimer disease and Lewy body disease. Anatomical differences and cognitive scores provide no dried fig or visual episode-frequency contrast.

The paper reviews structural, functional and other MRI measures used in Alzheimer disease diagnosis. Its emphasis is imaging and the diagnostic process, without a culinary exposure comparison or visual event follow-up in Parkinson disease.

The systematic review summarizes color vision findings in schizophrenia spectrum disorders. Color discrimination under testing and visual hallucination frequency are distinct. The article supplies neither a Parkinson cohort nor an ordinary dried fig exposure.
